bib.title: Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search", Yuichi Inoue, Kou Misaki, Yuki Imajuku, So Kuroki, Taishi Nakamura, Takuya Akiba (Sakana AI). NeurIPS 2025 spotlight; arXiv 2503.04412v5, 7 Nov 2025. Code: github.com/SakanaAI/treequest.

COVERAGE: 98,410 of 98,410 chars read (all 30 pages: body, limitations, appendices A-D, references skimmed). Tree-diagram figure text (Figs 7, 11) is garbled node numbers; ignored.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. AB-MCTS decides per node whether to go wider (new sample from the prompt) or deeper (refine an existing answer using external feedback). It does this with Thompson sampling over Bayesian posteriors and a GEN node that creates new "arms" on the fly. UCT is inapplicable because arms are generated dynamically.
 number: none
 setup: score r from an external evaluator R (tests, validation score); one LLM call per node.
 quote: "The UCT score is inapplicable to our AB-MCTS because GEN nodes make the problem fundamentally different from a standard multi-armed bandit problem" ; "the GEN node in AB-MCTS dynamically generates new arms."
 where: p5 (Sec 3.2)
2. Main result: AB-MCTS variants get the best average rank across the 6 benchmark/model settings (2.3 for -M, 2.7 for -A), against 3.5 for repeated sampling, 5.5 for sequential refinement and 4.2 for standard MCTS. Margins are small, often within error bars.
 number: avg rank 2.3 / 2.7 / 2.7 vs 3.5 / 5.5 / 4.2
 setup: LiveCodeBench, CodeContest, ARC-AGI (Pass@2); GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3; budget 2^7=128 LLM calls; n=5 runs (LCB), n=3 (CodeContest, ARC).
 quote: "AB-MCTS-M 38.9±1.9(2) 43.0±1.5(2) 40.6±1.0(1) 44.6±0.9(2) 12.3±1.2(4) 16.0±1.0(3) 2.3" and "Repeated Sampling 37.8±0.5(4) 40.7±1.9(6) 37.9±0.3(4) 43.2±0.9(5)15.0±1.0(1) 18.6±1.0(1)3.5"
 where: Table 1, p7
3. No single baseline wins everywhere. Repeated sampling is best on ARC-AGI. Standard MCTS is best on LiveCodeBench with DeepSeek-V3 (43.2). AB-MCTS is competitive across all tasks without tuning. The authors' argument is robustness, not dominance.
 number: ARC-AGI GPT-4o: RS 15.0, AB-MCTS-M 12.3, std MCTS 9.0, seq. refinement 8.7
 setup: as Table 1.
 quote: "Consistent with previous work [13], repeated sampling proves to be a strong baseline in our setup, indicating the importance of broad exploration for this task."
 where: p8; Table 1
4. ARC-AGI at a larger budget (DeepSeek-V3, up to 2^9=512 calls): AB-MCTS keeps improving while repeated sampling plateaus. Standard MCTS is lower.
 number: none given as a table; read off Fig 6 only
 quote: "the performance of AB-MCTS continues to improve substantially as the budget increases from 200 to 500, while the improvement rate of repeated sampling begins to plateau."
 where: pp9-10, Fig 6
5. MLE-Bench (GPT-4o, 3 low-complexity Kaggle tasks, one H100 for one hour per candidate, n=1): AB-MCTS-M has the best average rank (1.3). Only -M was run, because each candidate costs so much.
 number: avg rank 1.3 vs 3.0 / 2.3 / 3.3
 quote: "AB-MCTS-M 0.060 (2) 0.38 (1) 0.72 (1) 1.3" (Nomad2018 RMSLE, Spooky log loss, Pizza ROC AUC)
 where: Table 2, p7. Caveat: n=1, and Sequential Refinement wins Nomad2018 (0.059).
6. Vs progressive widening (PW, k n^alpha branching): a well-tuned PW matches AB-MCTS, but PW is hyperparameter-sensitive.
 number: PW 48.7 / 50.7 / 50.5 vs AB-MCTS-A Beta 51.8
 setup: LiveCodeBench, deepseek-v3-0324, budget 128, n=5.
 quote: "Pass@1 48.7±0.850.7±1.350.5±3.148.9±2.051.8±1.449.6±1.6" and "its effectiveness is highly sensitive to hyperparameters. For example, it produces the worst result with (k, α) = (1,0.45)."
 where: Table 4, App C.4
7. Fixed-width standard MCTS is sensitive to width w. A single w does not fit all.
 number: w=3: 0.429, w=5: 0.432, w=10: 0.402
 setup: LiveCodeBench, DeepSeek-V3, Pass@1.
 quote: "Pass@1 0.429±0.0180.432±0.0210.402±0.015"; "performance degrades with both smaller and larger widths"
 where: Table 6, C.8
8. Tree shape: AB-MCTS trees are wider than standard MCTS. AB-MCTS-M is mostly deep-ish with a long tail. AB-MCTS-A is much wider.
 number: M ~90% of non-leaf nodes have degree 1-3, tail up to 40; A has only ~30% at degree 1-3, tail >100.
 setup: LiveCodeBench, DeepSeek-V3, N=128.
 quote: "around 90% of its non-leaf nodes having a small degree (1–3)... degrees up to 40" ; "Low-degree nodes (1–3) account for only about 30% of its non-leaf nodes... degrees exceeding 100."
 where: C.7, Fig 12
9. Choosing between variants: -M uses MCMC (costly per selection but best quality). -A uses conjugate updates (cheap, wider, better for ARC-like tasks). The MCMC cost matters little when LLM or evaluation time dominates.
 number: none
 quote: "Reaching depth d requires d consecutive CONT choices, so deeper paths become geometrically less likely than wider expansions"
 where: C.5
10. Priors are non-critical. Pass@1 stays in a narrow band across prior sweeps.
 number: e.g. AB-MCTS-M 36.8-39.5
 setup: LiveCodeBench, GPT-4o, budget 2^4, 5 runs. Priors: mu_alpha~N(0.5,0.2^2), etc. Gaussian: m=0, kappa=1, nu=1, tau^2=0.1. Beta: alpha=beta=0.5.
 quote: "Across all tested ranges, the performance remains stable"
 where: A.6 Table 3; B.2. Differences are mostly within noise, so it is a weak test.
11. Multi-LLM AB-MCTS (preliminary): ARC-AGI-2 public eval set, 120 problems, budget 250, Pass@k. Repeated sampling with o4-mini reaches 23%, single-model AB-MCTS with o4-mini 27.5%, and mixing models passes 30%. Some problems no single model solved were solved by combining models.
 number: 23% / 27.5% / >30%; Pass@2 only 19.2%
 setup: o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-R1-0528; AB-MCTS-A; generator-selection algorithm II (one GEN node per LLM); temperature 0.6; Pass@k, not the official Pass@2 criterion.
 quote: "Repeated Sampling using the o4-mini model achieved a 23% Pass@k success rate on the public evaluation set, and the single-model AB-MCTS using o4-mini improved the success rate to 27.5%." ; "ultimately finding correct solutions for over 30% of the problems." ; "the Multi-LLM AB-MCTS achieved a Pass@2 of 19.2%."
 where: App D.2-D.3, pp27-30, Fig 13
12. Efficiency claim: AB-MCTS variants often reach the peak of repeated sampling at a lower budget. On LiveCodeBench they pull ahead from a budget of 2^3, and on CodeContest from 2^5.
 quote: "on LiveCodeBench (Figure 4 left), AB-MCTS starts to pull ahead of the baselines even with a small budget of 23." ; "AB-MCTS variants can reach the peak performance of repeated sampling substantially earlier in many cases"
 where: p8, p10
13. ARC-AGI-1 Pass@1 and Pass@2 give the same ranking.
 number: Pass@1 RS 14.0, AB-M 11.0, A-Gauss 13.0, A-Beta 12.7, std MCTS 8.0, seq 7.7
 quote: "the ranking of methods remains unchanged"
 where: Table 5, C.6. The text says the ranking is unchanged, but Table 5 shows A-Gauss ahead of A-Beta at Pass@1 and the reverse at Pass@2, so the claim is not literally true of AB-MCTS-A alone. It holds only at the level of "RS > AB > std MCTS/SR".

Method details worth keeping
- Algorithm 1: each iteration is select (descend until a GEN node is chosen), expand (the root generates from the prompt, a non-root node refines its answer using feedback), then back up the score. No rollout is needed because the score comes straight from the evaluator.
- AB-MCTS-M: a mixed-effects model per node, r = alpha_j + sigma_y*eps, alpha_j = mu_alpha + sigma_alpha*eps_j, fitted by MCMC. The GEN node is an unobserved new group, so its posterior stays wider, which drives exploration. Each child's group is its whole subtree.
- AB-MCTS-A: a CONT node aggregates the existing children. GEN and CONT each get an independent conjugate posterior (Gaussian normal-inverse-chi-squared, or Beta). Beta update: alpha_hat = alpha_0 + sum r, beta_hat = beta_0 + sum(1-r).
- Thompson sampling also allows parallel node expansion.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: "Our approach assumes the existence of a reliable score evaluator", and cost is counted only as API calls, not wall-clock or tokens (p10).
- Authors concede (D.3): a Pass@2 vs Pass@k gap on ARC-AGI-2 (19.2% vs 30%), so final-answer selection is unsolved.
- Small budgets (128 calls, 512 on ARC-AGI), n=3 to 5 runs, and wide error bars. Many Table 1 gaps are within a standard deviation. MLE-Bench has n=1, three easy tasks, and only AB-MCTS-M.
- Single-call coding and ARC tasks only. No math, no multi-step tool-using agents. The "refinement" is a rewrite of one program, not an agent trajectory.
- Models are dated: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 (and the 2025 frontier models in App D).
- Baselines: repeated sampling has no feedback cost and parallelises easily. The paper says so but does not measure wall-clock.
- Future work (C.10): difficulty-adaptive switching between -M and -A, and multi-LLM search.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Repeated sampling: Li et al. 2022 AlphaCode; Wang et al. 2023 self-consistency; Brown et al. 2024 Large Language Monkeys. Refinement with feedback: Madaan et al. 2024 Self-Refine; Shinn et al. 2024 Reflexion. LLM + MCTS: Zhou et al. 2024 LATS (the "standard MCTS" baseline config), Hao et al. 2023 RAP, Antoniades et al. 2025 SWE-Search, Ma et al. 2024 RepoUnderstander. Tree/Bayesian precedents: Li et al. 2025 CodeTree, Tang et al. 2024 (code repair as an exploration-exploitation tradeoff), Lee et al. 2025 Evolving Deeper LLM Thinking. Progressive widening: refs [36, 37]; Sokota et al. [38] abstraction refining. Snell et al. 2025 (compute-optimal test-time scaling) motivates difficulty-dependent strategy. Greenblatt 2024 (ARC-AGI with GPT-4o) is the repeated-sampling reference.

CODE (verbatim, App A.3.2, p16)
```
import pymc as pm
child_indices = [0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
rewards = [0.8, 0.8, 1.0, 0, 0.2, 0.3]
with pm.Model(coords=coords) as model:
    mu_alpha = pm.Normal("mu_alpha", mu=0.5, sigma=0.2)
    sigma_alpha = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_alpha", sigma=0.2)
    sigma_y = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_y", sigma=0.3)
    eps_j = pm.Normal("eps_j", mu=0, sigma=1, dims="child_idx")
    alpha = mu_alpha + eps_j * sigma_alpha
    r = pm.Normal("r", mu=alpha[child_indices], sigma=sigma_y, observed=rewards)
```
(Listing 1, the setup lines `coords = {"child_idx": [0, 1, 2]}` are omitted above.) GEN node (Listing 2):
```
eps_j_gen = pm.Normal("eps_j_gen", mu=0, sigma=1)
alpha_gen = mu_alpha + eps_j_gen * sigma_alpha
r_gen = pm.Normal("r_gen", mu=alpha_gen, sigma=sigma_y)
```

- Fig 2 (p4, AB-MCTS-M tree with posterior predictive curves per action; caption in the extraction, not in the figures.py output) and Fig 3 (p6): the example trees showing the GEN node (M) and the GEN/CONT split (A). They explain the Thompson-sampling choice faster than prose.
- Fig 4 (p8): success rate vs generation budget on LCB, CodeContest, ARC-AGI (GPT-4o); the main scaling plot.
- Fig 5 (p8): performance vs log(depth/width) of the tree; shows where each method sits.
- Fig 6 (p9): ARC-AGI to a budget of 512; repeated sampling plateaus.
- Fig 7 (p9) and Fig 11 (p22): example trees, AB-MCTS-M vs standard MCTS.
- Fig 12 (p25): node-degree distribution.
- Fig 13 (p28) and Fig 14 (p28): multi-LLM Pass@k on ARC-AGI-2 and LLM usage per problem.
